questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a painless ulcer on the hand with a central black eschar and surrounding gelatinous edema. Gram stain shows large gram-positive rods in chains. The most appropriate treatment is:
opts: Penicillin G 2 million units IV every 4 hours for 10-14 days
questions.exp: Cutaneous anthrax (Bacillus anthracis) with classic malignant pustule presentation. Systemic/severe cutaneous anthrax is treated with IV Penicillin G. Ciprofloxacin or doxycycline are used for post-exposure prophylaxis or mild cases.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with a non-healing ulcer on the nasal septum with destructive changes. KOH mount shows thick-walled muriform cells ('copper pennies'). Histopathology reveals pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with microabscesses. The causative organism is:
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis caused by Fonsecaea pedrosoi (most common causative agent). Characteristic muriform (sclerotic) bodies (Medlar bodies/copper pennies) are pathognomonic. The infection typically follows traumatic inoculation.

questions.q: A 22-year-old immunocompetent man presents with multiple grouped vesicles on an erythematous base over his chest, following a dermatomal distribution with severe burning pain. The antiviral of choice and its dosing regimen is:
opts: Acyclovir 200 mg 5 times daily for 5 days
Acyclovir 800 mg 5 times daily for 7 days
questions.exp: Herpes Zoster is treated with Acyclovir 800 mg 5 times daily (every 4 hours while awake) for 7 days. Valacyclovir 1g TDS for 7 days is equally effective but less commonly used at this dose in standard Indian guidelines.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man presents with a painless, indurated ulcer on the glans penis for 3 weeks. VDRL is reactive at 1:8 dilution and TPHA is positive. He is not allergic to penicillin. The treatment of choice is:
opts: Benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM single dose
Procaine penicillin 600,000 units IM daily for 10 days
questions.exp: Primary syphilis (chancre on glans with positive serology) is treated with Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose. This is the WHO and Indian NACO recommended first-line treatment.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man from rural India presents with hypopigmented anaesthetic patches over the trunk and thickened ulnar nerves. Slit skin smear shows 2+ AFB. The Ridley-Jopling classification and WHO treatment regimen applicable is:
questions.exp: Positive slit skin smear (2+ AFB) places this in the multibacillary (MB) spectrum, likely borderline lepromatous. MB-MDT (rifampicin + clofazimine + dapsone) for 12 months is the WHO-recommended treatment for MB leprosy.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with photosensitive facial rash in a butterfly distribution, oral ulcers, and arthritis. ANA is positive (1:320, homogeneous pattern). Anti-dsDNA is elevated. The most specific antibody for this diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Anti-Sm (anti-Smith) antibody is the most specific antibody for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), with specificity >95%. Anti-dsDNA is more sensitive. Anti-histone is associated with drug-induced lupus.

questions.q: A 60-year-old woman presents with tense bullae on normal and erythematous skin, predominantly on the flexures. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposits at the dermo-epidermal junction. The target antigen is:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) shows linear IgG and C3 at the BMZ on DIF. The target antigens are BP180 (BPAG2/Collagen XVII) and BP230 (BPAG1). BP180 is the more clinically significant antigen and correlates with disease severity.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with a pearly, translucent papule with telangiectasias on the nose, with a rolled border. Biopsy shows palisading basaloid cells with peripheral retraction artifact. The most appropriate treatment for a 1.5 cm lesion on the nose is:
opts: Standard wide local excision with 4 mm margins
questions.exp: Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) on the nose is in a high-risk H-zone. Mohs micrographic surgery provides the highest cure rate (>99%) with tissue-sparing for high-risk facial locations, recurrent tumors, or aggressive histologic subtypes.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents for botulinum toxin treatment of dynamic forehead lines. She is found to have previously undiagnosed myasthenia gravis. The contraindication to botulinum toxin in this patient is because it:
opts: Causes release of excess acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction
Blocks presynaptic acetylcholine release, exacerbating neuromuscular blockade
questions.exp: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins (SNAP-25 for type A), preventing presynaptic acetylcholine vesicle fusion and release at the neuromuscular junction. In myasthenia gravis, acetylcholine receptors are already compromised by antibodies, and botulinum toxin can precipitate or worsen muscle weakness.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman with severe acne unresponsive to multiple antibiotics is started on isotretinoin. The mechanism by which isotretinoin reduces sebum production is:
opts: Direct inhibition of 5-alpha reductase in sebaceous glands
Induction of sebocyte apoptosis via RAR-gamma activation
Competitive antagonism of androgen receptors in sebaceous glands
Inhibition of IL-1 alpha mediated comedogenesis
questions.exp: Isotretinoin (13-cis retinoic acid) induces apoptosis of sebocytes through activation of retinoic acid receptors (particularly RAR-gamma), leading to a 70-90% reduction in sebum production. This is its primary mechanism addressing all four pathogenic factors of acne.

questions.q: In the epidermis, the cell responsible for UV-induced immune suppression via cis-urocanic acid production is:
questions.exp: UV radiation converts trans-urocanic acid to cis-urocanic acid in the stratum corneum, which leads to immunosuppression partly by affecting Langerhans cell function and inducing regulatory T cells. Langerhans cells are the antigen-presenting dendritic cells of the epidermis.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with well-defined erythematous plaques with silvery scales on his elbows and knees. Auspitz sign is positive. His PASI score is 18. The most appropriate first-line systemic treatment for this patient is:
questions.exp: Methotrexate is the most widely used and cost-effective first-line systemic agent for moderate-to-severe psoriasis (PASI >10 or BSA >10%). It inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and has anti-inflammatory effects. It is preferred over cyclosporine for long-term use due to better safety profile.

questions.q: A 4-year-old child presents with intensely pruritic vesicles on the cheeks and extensor surfaces. The mother has atopic dermatitis. Serum IgE is markedly elevated. The most appropriate topical calcineurin inhibitor for this child is:
questions.exp: For atopic dermatitis in children 2-15 years, tacrolimus 0.03% ointment (not 0.1% which is for adults) is approved as a calcineurin inhibitor for moderate-severe disease. Pimecrolimus 1% cream is for mild-moderate AD. Tacrolimus 0.03% is the correct concentration for pediatric use.

questions.q: A 20-year-old woman from South India presents with progressive facial hyperpigmentation in a mask-like distribution aggravated by sun exposure and OCPs. Wood's lamp examination shows enhancement of the lesion. The most effective topical combination for melasma is:
opts: Hydroquinone 4% + tretinoin 0.05% + fluocinolone acetonide 0.01% (modified Kligman's formula)
questions.exp: The modified Kligman's formula (triple combination: hydroquinone 4% + tretinoin 0.05% + fluocinolone acetonide 0.01%) is the gold standard and most evidence-based topical treatment for melasma. It is available as Tri-Luma cream and shows superior efficacy to monotherapy.

questions.q: A 45-year-old HIV-positive man presents with multiple painless papules with central umbilication scattered over the face. CD4 count is 85 cells/microL. The most effective treatment for individual lesions is:
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum in immunocompromised HIV patients tends to be extensive. Cryotherapy is the most effective and widely used physical treatment for individual lesions. In HIV patients, HAART to restore immunity is the definitive approach, but individual lesions are best treated with cryotherapy or curettage.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, puffy fingers, and progressive skin tightening of the fingers, hands, and face. ANA is positive with a centromere pattern. The most likely diagnosis and its associated esophageal complication is:
opts: Diffuse systemic sclerosis; esophageal stricture due to acid reflux
Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST); lower esophageal dysmotility
Mixed connective tissue disease; esophageal web
questions.exp: Anti-centromere antibody is characteristic of Limited cutaneous SSc (lcSSc/CREST syndrome: Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia). Lower esophageal smooth muscle replacement by fibrosis causes dysmotility, GERD, and Barrett's esophagus.

questions.q: A patient on MDT for borderline lepromatous leprosy develops Type 1 (reversal) lepra reaction with new nerve involvement. The most appropriate management is:
opts: Continue MDT and add prednisolone 40 mg/day tapering over 12 weeks
Stop clofazimine and continue rifampicin and dapsone with thalidomide
Stop all MDT and start prednisolone alone
Continue MDT and add thalidomide 100 mg/day
questions.exp: Type 1 (reversal) lepra reaction is treated with prednisolone 40 mg/day with gradual taper over a minimum of 12 weeks. MDT must NEVER be stopped during reactions. Thalidomide is used for Type 2 (ENL) reactions, not Type 1.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman presents with flaccid bullae that rupture easily, leaving raw erosions on the oral mucosa and trunk. Nikolsky sign is positive. DIF shows intercellular IgG deposits in a 'chicken wire' pattern. The predominant autoantigen in mucosal-dominant disease is:
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris (PV) predominantly involving mucosal surfaces is mediated primarily by anti-desmoglein 3 antibodies. Anti-desmoglein 1 causes pemphigus foliaceus (superficial blisters, no mucosal involvement). Both antigens are targeted in mucocutaneous PV.

questions.q: A 65-year-old male presents with a pigmented lesion on the sole of the foot with variegated pigmentation, irregular borders, and diameter of 2 cm. Biopsy reveals malignant melanocytes with Breslow thickness 3.2 mm. The single most important prognostic factor is:
questions.exp: Breslow thickness (depth of invasion in millimeters from the granular layer to the deepest melanoma cell) is the single most important prognostic factor for cutaneous melanoma and determines T-staging in the AJCC system. Clark level is used as a secondary criterion in T1 lesions only.

questions.q: A dermatologist is performing a punch biopsy for suspected dermatomyositis. The most diagnostically useful site to biopsy is:
opts: Active skin lesion on the face (heliotrope rash area)
questions.exp: Gottron's papules (violaceous flat-topped papules over the knuckles) are pathognomonic of dermatomyositis. Biopsy of Gottron's papules shows interface dermatitis with vacuolar change, which is more specific than facial lesions and provides the highest diagnostic yield for skin biopsy in dermatomyositis.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman with lichen planus is started on hydroxychloroquine. The mandatory monitoring investigation during treatment is:
opts: Ophthalmologic examination including visual field testing annually
questions.exp: Hydroxychloroquine can cause irreversible retinopathy (bull's eye maculopathy). Baseline ophthalmologic examination and annual screening with visual field testing and optical coherence tomography (OCT) is mandatory, especially after 5 years of use or with cumulative dose >5 mg/kg/day.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man presents with painful punched-out ulcers on the genitals and multiple oral aphthous ulcers. Pathergy test is positive. He also has hypopyon uveitis. The pathological basis of this condition involves:
opts: Type IV hypersensitivity to HSV antigens
Neutrophil hyperreactivity and vasculitis of small vessels
B-cell mediated autoimmunity against mucosal antigens
Mast cell degranulation in response to thermal stimuli
questions.exp: Behcet's disease is a systemic vasculitis characterized by neutrophil hyperreactivity, hyperfunction, and enhanced migration. The pathergy phenomenon (non-specific hyperreactivity of skin to minor trauma) reflects this neutrophil dysfunction. Small vessel vasculitis affects multiple organ systems including eyes, skin, and mucosae.

questions.q: A 16-year-old boy presents with fish-scale like thickening over the extensor surfaces with sparing of the flexures, worse in winter. His father has a similar condition. The genetic defect in this most common inherited ichthyosis is:
questions.exp: Ichthyosis vulgaris (most common inherited ichthyosis, AD inheritance) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the FLG gene encoding filaggrin. This leads to reduced keratohyalin granules (seen on histology), impaired skin barrier, and association with atopic disease. TGM1 mutations cause lamellar ichthyosis; steroid sulfatase deficiency causes X-linked ichthyosis.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man presents with a rapidly enlarging, firm, dome-shaped nodule on the cheek that developed over 6 weeks with a central keratinous plug. Biopsy shows a cup-shaped architecture with keratin-filled crater and well-differentiated squamous epithelium. The best next step is:
opts: Observe for 2 months as spontaneous resolution is expected
questions.exp: Keratoacanthoma (KA) classically regresses spontaneously, but due to its histologic resemblance to well-differentiated SCC and inability to reliably distinguish the two on biopsy alone, full excision with clear margins is recommended. This allows complete histologic assessment and provides definitive treatment.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman on long-term acyclovir for recurrent herpes labialis develops acute renal failure. The mechanism of acyclovir-induced nephrotoxicity is:
opts: Direct tubular cell toxicity via reactive oxygen species generation
Intratubular crystallization of acyclovir in collecting ducts
Inhibition of aquaporin channels in renal tubules
questions.exp: Acyclovir is poorly soluble and can crystallize in renal tubules (particularly collecting ducts) when given at high doses or with inadequate hydration, causing obstructive nephropathy. Prevention involves adequate hydration and slow IV infusion. Dose adjustment is needed in pre-existing renal impairment.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of symmetrical proximal muscle weakness, dysphagia, and violaceous discoloration around the eyes. CPK is 2500 U/L. The autoantibody MOST strongly associated with underlying malignancy is:
questions.exp: Anti-TIF1-gamma (transcription intermediary factor 1-gamma) antibody is most strongly associated with cancer-associated dermatomyositis, particularly in patients >40 years. Anti-Jo-1 associates with antisynthetase syndrome/ILD; anti-MDA5 with rapidly progressive ILD and amyopathic DM; anti-Mi-2 with classical DM and good prognosis.

questions.q: A 35-year-old male leprosy patient on MDT develops sudden onset of painful red nodules over the thighs and forearms with fever and arthralgia. Smear shows BI of 4+. The drug of choice for recurrent episodes of this reaction is:
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL) or Type 2 lepra reaction occurs in lepromatous/borderline lepromatous leprosy. Thalidomide is the drug of choice for recurrent or chronic ENL due to its anti-TNF-alpha mechanism. Prednisolone is used for acute ENL or when thalidomide is contraindicated (women of childbearing age).

questions.q: A 19-year-old woman presents with painful grouped vesicles on the vulva with bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy and fever for the first episode. The gold standard diagnostic test is:
opts: Tzanck smear showing multinucleated giant cells
HSV PCR from swab of the lesion
questions.exp: HSV PCR (polymerase chain reaction) from lesion swabs is the gold standard for diagnosing genital herpes, with sensitivity >95% and high specificity. It can differentiate HSV-1 from HSV-2. Viral culture is more specific but less sensitive (70-80%) and slower. Tzanck smear is rapid but non-specific (no type differentiation).

questions.q: A 24-year-old man presents with a painless vulvar ulcer with a bright red, velvety granulomatous base and raised irregular edges. No lymphadenopathy. Giemsa stain of tissue smear shows 'Donovan bodies' within macrophages. The treatment of choice is:
opts: Doxycycline 100 mg BD for minimum 3 weeks
Benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM weekly for 3 weeks
Cotrimoxazole 960 mg BD for minimum 3 weeks
questions.exp: Donovanosis (granuloma inguinale) is caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. Donovan bodies are intracytoplasmic inclusions within macrophages. Doxycycline 100 mg BD for minimum 3 weeks (or until complete healing) is the first-line WHO treatment. Azithromycin 1g weekly for 3 weeks is an alternative.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman on long-term prednisolone for pemphigus vulgaris develops painful ulceration of the oral mucosa and esophagus. KOH smear shows pseudohyphae and budding yeast. The drug of choice for esophageal candidiasis is:
opts: Nystatin oral suspension 5 mL 4 times daily for 14 days
Fluconazole 200 mg loading then 100 mg daily for 14-21 days
Itraconazole oral solution 200 mg daily for 7 days
questions.exp: Esophageal candidiasis in immunosuppressed patients requires systemic antifungal therapy. Fluconazole is the drug of choice per IDSA guidelines, with loading dose 200 mg then 100 mg daily for 14-21 days. Nystatin only covers superficial oral candidiasis and is not effective for esophageal disease.

questions.q: A 42-year-old man presents with a chronic plaque on the nasal tip with central scarring and peripheral hyperpigmentation. Biopsy shows tuberculoid granulomas with Langhans giant cells, caseous necrosis, and AFB on Ziehl-Neelsen stain. Mantoux is 20 mm. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Lupus vulgaris is the most common form of cutaneous TB in India, presenting as a chronic plaque typically on the face (nose, cheek). The apple jelly nodules on diascopy, central scarring, and tuberculoid granulomas with occasional AFB are characteristic. Scrofuloderma arises from underlying lymph node/bone TB; verrucosa cutis has a verrucous surface from exogenous inoculation.
